title: Dr. Kristen Park:
headline: A place for care where families do not have to explain: the doctor who treats the children, and why no disorder gets left behind.
story: Dr. Park is the only doctor in the four films who treats the children. She opens on a promise of care: “you don't have to explain what's going on.” Then what these disorders do, in simple words, where the research stands, and what a family gets at the Center of Excellence, including her own honest limit: we can't replace your pediatrician down the street.
She ends on the full family of disorders: the less common ones must not be left behind. It must feel warm, clear and hopeful. Not a dry medical lesson. No promise that every family gets a visit.

Frame tighter than the camera did: the 4K source gives you room.

Never say or show that GRIN disorders can be prevented, are anyone's fault, or have a cure soon.
No shots of people eating. No childcare-room shots unless Nick confirms consent.
Do not reuse a B-roll shot that another researcher film uses.

transcript:
Auto-transcript of MVI_0943.MP4 (Interview 11). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Labels are automatic: lines marked Interviewer are often Dr. Park.
[02:09] Okay. My name is Kristen Park. I am a child neurologist and an epilepsy specialist who also works with a variety of neurogenetic conditions, including glutamate receptor disorders.
[02:22] I've been involved with this organization, the organization surrounding that since about 2019 when I went to the conference in Atlanta.
[02:33] And since that time, I've been a part of our registry and an attendee at the conferences and caring for patients with this diagnosis.
[03:16] So I think that's one level of connection, but also think it's important for families to connect with each other to get a sense that there is hope, that there is discovery going on, that there is progress being made.
[03:41] You know, family advocacy groups and these types of organizations are really starting to drive the research world.
[03:51] They are contributing. They are the focus and now being kind of brought into the discussions in a way that they haven't been over the last 20 to 50 years.
[04:02] And so I think they are an important member of the group of people that needs to come together to work on finding treatments.
[04:14] Interviewer: What do you hope families better understand about the priorities?
[04:20] Yeah, I hope that they understand that it's in a variety of different directions, that it's on a number of different levels.
[04:29] It's on the level of the individual child and what we can help them with.
[04:34] It's on the level of us being forces behind science policy and funding and working with the NIH.
[04:43] And it's also on the level of working with pharmaceutical companies who are developing new compounds and new techniques that we're kind of moving forward in a broad scope of directions that will ultimately get us to where we want to be.
[05:00] And that people are working all the time, even though it feels a bit slow.
[05:06] I also think that within the rare disease community, the common phrase that I like to use is that a rising tide is going to lift all boats.
[05:15] We are all in this together. Many of these things that we are working on, we've gotten help from other organizations.
[05:22] The discoveries that are being made in one field are also going to be put to bear on this problem and that all of us are needed to work together to move it forward.
[05:44] Yeah, I think they really give a sense of invigoration to all the people that come.
[05:50] It reminds us of what we're doing and why we're doing it.
[05:54] It helps us to feel appreciated, to feel connected to what we're working for.
[06:03] I think it helps the families to gain a better understanding of what's happening so that they can stay engaged and they can continue to take the steps that they need to get involved.
[06:18] I think if you don't do that in person, you lose a lot of the flavor and the camaraderie and the joy and the sense of community that happens when you're all in the same place together.
[06:42] It's a great place to meet a bunch of people that are really smart, that know what they're doing, that have resources to help you along the way with whatever question it is that you are trying to answer.
[06:58] It's a really committed community of organizers and leaders in science and in research to help move the needle for you.
[07:17] Interviewer: Can you talk a little bit about the Center of Excellence?
[07:21] I think there are many groups who are pursuing this kind of a treatment model where because it's such a rare condition and not everyone is going to know about it,
[07:35] you can concentrate that knowledge in places where you have somebody who's invested in taking care of those kids and those people.
[07:43] We have decided to do that model where we care for all people with glutamate receptor disorders and serve as a place for expertise, a place for research, a place for care where you don't have to explain what's going on.
[08:04] You just have people that know how to help your family member.
[08:08] I think we in Colorado are the first one in the US.
[08:13] There's one in the Netherlands.
[08:15] There's one opening in Boston.
[08:17] The goal would be for all of those people to combine their efforts to standardize some of the care and some of the recommendations to learn from those patients and say,
[08:27] what can we do better the next time?
[08:29] I haven't seen anybody who has this symptom, but let me talk to my colleagues.
[08:34] Oh, yes, now we've got that, and this is what they did.
[08:37] Let's try that.
[08:38] If you build that network, then you are advancing, again, care on that individual and group level, which is what we all want.
[08:47] Interviewer: What can families expect when they're visiting the Center of Excellence, and how can they do it if they want to?
[08:53] I think they can expect people to know what their challenges are, to know what their diagnosis is, to bring together a team of experts.
[09:03] Usually, that's more than just a neurologist or a geneticist.
[09:07] It's going to be a group of people that are going to be centered around what the common challenges are.
[09:14] They can expect those people to be allies for them, to support them, to provide advice, to help with decision-making.
[09:23] We obviously can't replace someone, your pediatrician down the street or the neurologist that you can get to in an emergency,
[09:31] but we are definitely a resource for the up-to-date care and recommendations that might be difficult to get at home.
[09:56] Usually, people get a referral from their local provider, either their pediatrician, their internal medicine doctor if they're an adult, or their genetics person.
[10:24] Then, we bring them in. It's a long visit. It's a lot of people to see, but it usually ends up being very informative
[10:32] and really helpful for the families that can get to us.
[10:53] I think our body is a complex, yet kind of redundant system.
[11:01] It has a number of different things that kind of fall together in different groups that perform similar functions.
[11:09] We've put all of these together into the group of Ionotropic Glutamate Receptors, meaning that they respond to glutamate,
[11:17] they act quickly, and they help to send signals within the brain.
[11:22] They come in different families. Each family has subgroups. They combine themselves in different ways to make these channels.
[11:30] At the end of the day, basically, we know that having genetic changes in how these channels are built
[11:38] ends up affecting how the brain is able to communicate amongst itself and to send messages to the rest of the body.
[11:47] Most of these conditions kind of share some common features, including neurodevelopmental issues, autism, language issues, seizures,
[11:59] and those are really tough things because they are part of our brain and what makes us kind of unique and what makes us human.
[12:18] It kind of takes a smart group of people to figure out what those things are.
[12:23] I think that each of these receptors is a complex unit composed of multiple different parts.
[12:45] I think the most common thing that we see is variations within Grin2B, but there are other ionotropic glutamate receptor families.
[13:09] I think we are wanting to make sure that those ones that are less common don't get left behind
[13:18] because they may have the secrets to unlocking things for the whole family of disorders.
[13:25] (first take of the name - do not use)
[14:09] I think one of the great things about Cure Grin is that they recognize that this is a collection of a number of different diagnoses.
[14:19] It needs an umbrella organization to make sure that the discoveries and the research and the science gets shared
[14:29] amongst the ones that are the most common and have the most money behind them as well as the ones that we haven't even discovered yet
[14:37] or just discovered a few years ago.
[14:41] We think that because all of these work together in our body that we need to work together to figure them out
[14:48] and to make new treatments and new scientific discoveries so that we can help the people and move the field forward.
